beats.care: If RBI's plans are clear, your loan rates and prices move less by surprise. That matters most if you live month to month.
beats.what: The Hindu's editorial says the Nobel-winning work of Robert Hall and Michael Woodford matters especially now, and holds lessons for India's policymakers.
beats.why: Their research shows that what households and firms expect about the future changes how they spend, price and borrow today.

cards.body: The paper argues the winners' big idea, that expectations about the future ripple back into today's decisions, fits a world hit by sudden supply shocks. It says Indian policymakers have already learnt some of these lessons, but households and businesses decide with more confidence when medium-term policy is clear and stable.
cards.title: Ripples from the future
cards.verdict: Steady, predictable policy is itself a tool against inflation.

cards.body: If shops and workers expect prices to keep rising, they raise prices and ask for higher pay early. That can keep inflation going even after the original shock fades. A trusted target helps stop that loop.
cards.title: why do expectations push prices?

cards.body: The editorial also notes that many households live hand to mouth, with no savings to absorb a shock. For them, a sudden jump in fuel or food prices hurts at once, which is why calm, predictable policy matters.
The economics prize isn't one of Alfred Nobel's original prizes. Sweden's central bank created it in 1968, and it was first given in 1969.

cards.q: What should RBI focus on now?

opts: Clear, stable policy shapes what people expect
cards.q: What is the editorial's main lesson for India?
cards.why: When people trust where policy is headed, they plan calmly, which helps keep prices steady.

hook: Can a *promise about tomorrow* cool prices today?

learn.t: RBI's 4% inflation target, set by law in 2016, works partly by anchoring what people expect prices to do next.
